                                           PROJECT NO. 58000

 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                                     §
                                                                  PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                                 §
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY IN                            §
                                                                                 OF TEXAS
 THE ERCOT REGION                                         §

          AEP COMPANIES’ COMMENTS ON PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION

                                           I.       INTRODUCTION

        AEP Texas Inc. (AEP Texas) and Electric Transmission Texas, LLC (ETT) (collectively,

the AEP Companies) respectfully submit these comments in response to the Public Utility

Commission of Texas’ (the Commission) Proposal for Publication (PFP) for amended 16 Texas

Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.192, relating to Transmission Service Rates, § 25.193, relating

to Distribution Service Provider (DSP) Transmission Cost Recovery Factor (TCRF), and new 16

TAC § 25.252, relating to Large Load Customer Tariffs, approved at the July 9, 2026 Open

Meeting.1 The AEP Companies appreciate the Commission’s ongoing efforts to facilitate the

rulemakings arising from Senate Bill (SB) 6, enacted by the 89th Texas Legislature. As the

SB 6-related rulemakings are completed and new rules are implemented, the AEP Companies are

interested in ensuring that interrelated issues and requirements set forth in the new or amended

rules are aligned as necessary to provide consistency with the planning for, interconnection and

operation of, and costs related to providing service for load customers of 75MW or greater (Large

Loads). For instance, the evaluation of transmission cost recovery addressed in Project No. 584842

and the standards for interconnecting large load customers in ERCOT that are being established in

Project No. 584813 impact the subject matter of Project No. 58000.


         1
           To the extent any issues discussed herein pertain exclusively to retail service, ETT takes no position on
those issues.
         2
           Evaluation of Transmission Cost Recovery, Project No. 58484 (pending).
         3
           Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA 37.0561, Project No. 58481
(pending).

Project No. 58000                                                                       AEP Companies Comments
                                                         1
             The AEP Companies support the Commission’s objective in this project of aligning

    cost responsibility with the loads that drive transmission and distribution investment while

    ensuring that implementation of these changes provides regulatory clarity, preserves

    appropriate cost recovery mechanisms, and protects existing customers from unintended cost

    shifts. The AEP Companies’ comments focus on maintaining the intent of SB 6 while

    providing greater clarity, administrative feasibility, and regulatory certainty. The AEP

    Companies offer suggestions to some provisions of the PFP to clarify that cost responsibility

    remains appropriately assigned to Large Load customers while avoiding unintended impacts

    on existing transmission cost recovery mechanisms, treatment of transmission investments,

    and other customer classes. AEP Companies have also identified several provisions in the PFP

    that could create potential unintended consequences for existing transmission cost recovery

    mechanisms unrelated to non-Large Load customers and have recommended clarifications and

    specific revisions to ensure that Large Load transmission interconnection costs are addressed

    separately from broader transmission investments, consistent with SB 6.


                    II.    RESPONSES TO QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT

        The AEP Companies provide responses to the Commission’s specific questions included

in the PFP below.

    1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions
       be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
       different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

        No. A minimum demand charge ensures that Large Load customers are responsible for the

transmission investment caused by their demand on the system, rather than only being responsible

for their energy usage. Implementing minimum billing demand provisions is consistent with the

directives in Governor Abbott’s June 10, 2026 letter to the Commission and ERCOT. The AEP

Project No. 58000                                                         AEP Companies Comments
                                                2
 Companies support a minimum billing demand provision that applies to all Large Load customers

in the same manner and is based on each customer’s contracted peak demand, not its non-

coincident peak (NCP) demand. This approach will ensure that all Large Load customers are

equally accountable to the capacity that they have reserved and align to the actual driver of costs

because transmission and distribution infrastructure is planned and built to serve the capacity that

a customer reserves. A utility commits capital based on contracted peak demand, not on what the

customer happens to draw in any given interval. Under an NCP scenario, a Large Load could

reserve substantial capacity, causing the serving utility to build significant infrastructure to meet

that maximum load. If a Large Load customer ramps slowly or underutilizes their contracted

demand, that customer could pay far below the cost of the infrastructure dedicated to serving them,

resulting in other classes being allocated those costs. The use of contracted peak demand better

matches the cost to the customer who requested the level of service driving the infrastructure

investment.

    2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
          a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
          b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
          c. extended to a longer time period?

        In Project No. 58484, the AEP Companies provided comments on minimum billing

demand contract terms. As described in those comments, the other AEP affiliates have Large Load

tariffs in place that include fixed contract periods of 12-20 years. The AEP Companies support a

minimum billing demand period that is consistent with cost-causation arguments and the overall

recent policy directives to balance Large Load development and non-Large Load customer

interests. One challenge the AEP Companies have identified with the minimum billing demand

construct currently set forth in the PFP, as compared to its affiliates’ tariffs, is that the PFP does

not include some other key provisions of a Large Load tariff such as a collateral requirement and


Project No. 58000                                                            AEP Companies Comments
                                                  3
 defined exit fee with a notice requirement that helps ensure that other ratepayers are held harmless

if a Large Load customer ceases taking service before the minimum billing demand period expires.

The AEP Companies recommend that the Commission consider adding these key provisions to the

rule as discussed further below and in the AEP Companies’ comments in Project No. 58484.

    3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
       lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
       load minimum billing demand:
          a. reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand
              is some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum
              NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline
              in phases over the years, and how?
          b. be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large
              load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
              customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
              year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
              weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
              over the years, and how?

        As stated in the response to Question 1, the AEP Companies believe the minimum billing

demand should be based on contracted peak demand. It is a floor the customer pays regardless of

actual usage. Transmission and distribution infrastructure is planned and constructed to serve the

capacity reserved by the customer, and contracted peak demand provides the most direct link

between the customer's service request and the investment required to serve that request.

Accordingly, the AEP Companies do not support basing the minimum billing demand on a

measure lower than contracted peak demand.

        Ideally, the minimum billing demand would be based on the contract peak demand until

such time that the Large Load customer’s 12CP demand exceeds the minimum contract demand.

In that instance there is no need for the adoption of an NCP minimum billing demand or ratchet

given that the average prior year 12CP is based on a 100% ratchet. If the Commission were to

adopt an NCP-based approach, the AEP Companies believe a ratchet mechanism would be

preferable to relying solely on actual usage because it would establish a billing floor that Large

Project No. 58000                                                           AEP Companies Comments
                                                 4
 Loads must pay regardless of usage and reduce the potential for a customer to lower its obligation

through temporary curtailment after establishing peak demand level.

        The AEP Companies do not recommend a weighted average minimum billing demand.

Such an approach would add complexity without providing meaningful improvement in cost

causation or cost recovery as compared to either a contracted peak demand framework or an

NCP-based framework.

    4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as
       an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
       Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
       electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
       cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include
       applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large
       computational loads.

        Separate rate treatment for large computational load should take into account applicable

Texas statutes and Commission rules that govern rates, rate classes, and tariffs. Under PURA §

36.003(b), a rate may not be unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory but must be

sufficient, equitable, and consistent in application to each class of consumer. In addition, PURA §

36.003(c) prohibits an electric utility from (1) granting an unreasonable preference or advantage

concerning rates to a person in a classification; (2) subjecting a person in a classification to an

unreasonable prejudice or disadvantage concerning rates; or (3) establishing or maintaining an

unreasonable difference concerning rates between localities or between classes of service.

Separate rate treatment for computational loads, such as data centers, would create a new

classification of a consumer and rates charged to that new classification would need to be evaluated

under PURA § 36.003. If separate rate treatment for computational loads was implemented, large

load requirements may not be consistently applied to all customers meeting the applicable

threshold unless the Commission determines there is a reasonable basis for treating computational

loads differently than other Large Loads. Section 32.101 of PURA requires electric utilities to file

Project No. 58000                                                           AEP Companies Comments
                                                 5
 official tariffs showing all rates, rules, and classifications with each regulatory authority. An

electric utility may not directly or indirectly charge, demand, or receive from a person a greater or

lesser compensation for a service provided or to be provided by the utility than the compensation

prescribed by the applicable tariff filed under Section 32.101.4 The statutory definition of “rate”

encompasses a tariff5 while Commission rules more specifically address a tariff as a utility’s

schedule containing all rates and charges stated separately by type of service.6 Commission rules

also define rate class as a group of customers taking electric service under the same rate schedule.7

The AEP Companies also note that SB 6 does not require separate rate treatment for a specific

subset of Large Load customers, rather it addresses all loads of 75 MW or greater. The Commission

could incorporate any rate-related specifics of large computational loads into an existing rate

schedule with additional distinct terms and conditions that applied to these loads.

    5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
       transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to
       serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

        No, the definition of Transmission Interconnection Costs should not be broadened to

include transmission projects identified through the batch study process. As discussed further

below, the AEP Companies believe the definition should be limited to customer-specific

interconnection facilities and should be clarified to apply to facilities constructed solely to

interconnect a Large Load customer to the transmission system. Broader transmission network

upgrades identified through transmission planning processes provide system-wide benefits and

serve multiple current or future customers over time. Expanding the definition to include such

facilities would make it very challenging for transmission providers to assign network upgrades to


        4
          PURA § 36.004(a).
        5
          PURA § 31.002(15).
        6
          16 TAC § 25.5(130).
        7
          16 TAC § 25.5(100).

Project No. 58000                                                            AEP Companies Comments
                                                 6
 specific customers. Accordingly, the AEP Companies recommend a narrower definition that

balances the intent of SB 6 to protect non-Large Load customers while preserving established

transmission cost recovery frameworks and supporting continued investment in the transmission

system.

    6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of
       whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity,
       how should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments
       and transmission planning studies?

        If Large Loads are able to receive a capacity allocation, as contemplated in the Batch

process at ERCOT, that allocation should be treated as firm load (i.e., taken/consumed) in resource

adequacy reports, assessments, and transmission planning studies, regardless of whether the Large

Load has energized or is fully utilizing its allocated capacity, unless the Large Load reduces its

request or is removed from the system. This approach is similar to the manner in which ERCOT

performs transmission planning currently, by including all approved Regional Planning Group

projects in future planning models, even before those facilities are energized.


                    III.   COMMENTS ON PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION

    A. § 25.192 Transmission Service Rates

§ 25.192(b)(2) – If the Commission intends for all Large Loads, including behind-the-meter loads

to be allocated costs based on the peak demand they could draw from the system, the definition of

ERCOT 12CP would need to be revised to clarify that all transmission-voltage connected loads,

including behind-the-meter loads, are accounted for when measuring the load that the transmission

system must be planned and sized to serve. While behind-the-meter loads are often served by

resources located behind the same meter, the system is planned and constructed to reliably serve

its customers based on situations where generation or load exists without the other. Thus, co-



Project No. 58000                                                           AEP Companies Comments
                                                 7
 locations can still necessitate network upgrades. There are also situations, such as planned and

forced outages, that could require those loads to be served from the ERCOT system.

        Proposed Redline

        (2)     DSP 12 coincident peak (12CP) load -- The average of the 12 demand values of a
                DSP that are coincident with the ERCOT 12CP intervals determined from the total
                demand of all customers within the ERCOT region connected to a DSP, including
                load served at transmission voltage, wholesale storage load, behind the meter
                loads, and block load transfers, but excluding export flows.


§ 25.192(b)(4) – The term ERCOT 12CP intervals is proposed to be defined as “[t]he set of 12

30-minute intervals…” Currently, transmission billing in ERCOT is based on 15-minute intervals,

and AEP Texas’ meters are set to poll data at that interval, as noted in AEP Companies’ comments

filed in Project Nos. 58481 and 58484. AEP Texas continues to support the use of the existing 15-

minute interval as ERCOT transmission billing transitions to a 12CP structure. This support stems

from concern that collecting 30-minute data at the metering level would require remotely

reprogramming all polling meters by broadcasting a new meter program to them, which could

cause meters to perform a “master reset.” Master resets cause existing meter data to be lost. The

market is not set up to handle the transmission and distribution service providers sending a meter

change while using the same meter number and resetting the reading back to zero. For this reason,

AEP Texas has never changed the meter program remotely in this manner. Non-remote changes

would require personnel to visit every meter, which would require a significant time frame for

implementation. If a 30-minute interval is approved by the Commission, it should allow DSPs to

aggregate the 15-minute interval data that meters are already programmed to poll into 30-minute

intervals.




Project No. 58000                                                         AEP Companies Comments
                                                8
           Proposed Redline

          (4)   ERCOT 12CP intervals -- The set of 12 30-minute intervals composed of the
                ERCOT system monthly peak demand interval for each of the 12 calendar months
                from October 1 of one year through September 30 of the subsequent year, inclusive.
                DSPs using meters with a 15-minute data interval should aggregate that meter data
                into 30-minute intervals pairing the 1st and 2nd intervals of a given hour, and the 3rd
                and 4th intervals of a given hour.


§§ 25.192(b)(13) and 25.252(b)(5) define the term Transmission Interconnection Costs, which

is used in § 25.192(e)(6) regarding the ability of utilities to include transmission interconnection

costs in rates and in § 25.252(c)(2) to specify Cost in Aid of Construction (CIAC) for Large Load

customers. The AEP Companies recommend revisions to the rule language to clarify that this term

is intended to address retail customer-specific interconnection facilities that are constructed solely

to serve a Large Load customer and that would not otherwise be required absent that retail

customer's request. As written, this definition uses the wording, “…transmission-level customers,

or a distinct set of transmission-level customers…” While the AEP Companies believe that the

intention is to capture retail Large Load customers, the definition could be interpreted to more

broadly include other wholesale transmission customers rather than retail loads. § 25.5(141)

defines

       Transmission service customer -- A transmission service provider, distribution service
       provider, river authority, municipally-owned utility, electric cooperative, power generation
       company, retail electric provider, federal power marketing agency, exempt wholesale
       generator, qualifying facility, power marketer, or other person whom the commission has
       determined to be eligible to be a transmission service customer. A retail customer, as defined
       in this section, may not be a transmission service customer.

Transmission service customers are by definition “transmission-level customers,” and their

interconnection is generally specified in § 25.195. The AEP Companies do not believe that SB 6

intended to extend the limitation of cost recovery to non-retail transmission service customers, like


Project No. 58000                                                             AEP Companies Comments
                                                   9
 generators and other utilities. Therefore, the AEP Companies propose narrowing the definition of

transmission interconnection costs proposed in this rulemaking to capture retail loads only, in

particular retail Large Loads (those in excess of 75 MW). The proposed revision below also ties

in with similar language that was proposed in Project No. 58481 for Direct Interconnection Costs

in hopes of adding further clarity to this definition.

        Proposed Redline

        25.192(b)(13) and § 25.252(b)(5)      Transmission interconnection costs -- All Direct
        Interconnection Costs (as described in 25.194(f)(9)(A)) costs associated with the facilities
        required to physically interconnect or upgrade the interconnection of a transmission-level
        retail load customer of 75MW or greater, or a distinct set of transmission-level retail load
        customers of 75MW or greater, to the existing transmission network, including
        interconnection lines, substation additions or modifications, and associated equipment
        necessary to establish or modify service.


§ 25.192(e)(6) – The AEP Companies recognize the importance of directly assigning costs that

benefit one customer directly to that specific customer and understand that one of the goals of SB

6 was to protect other rate classes from costs driven by the growth of Large Loads on the ERCOT

system. While this has historically been the practice of the AEP Companies on a smaller scale with

smaller loads than these Large Loads, the practice of taking very large CIACs will have a greater

impact on utilities’ legal right to earn a return on their investment. Even when a customer provides

a CIAC, it is the utility that bears the risk associated with construction as well as the long-term

operation and maintenance of the facilities. This portion of electric facilities covered by CIAC will

be increasing outside of a utility’s rate base, resulting in an inability to earn a return while incurring

additional costs associated with those assets. The construction risks and associated O&M costs

will be increasing at the same time utilities are faced with the need to raise significant capital to

meet the needs of customers in Texas. This shift could negatively impact utilities’ credit ratings



Project No. 58000                                                               AEP Companies Comments
                                                   10
 and ability to procure capital. These payments for large construction projects have potential to

erode the financial health of the utilities without the opportunity to earn a return on the investment.


§ 25.192(e)(7) – The AEP Companies request clarification as to whether this language is additional

to existing rate filing package requirement for investor-owned utilities (IOU)-TDUs filing a base

rate case. The AEP Companies believe that information used to determine the prudence of capital

expenditures belongs properly in a base rate case, and this information is already captured in the

requirements of Schedule M for IOU TDUs. The AEP Companies request that Schedule M be

deemed an acceptable format in which to provide this information for review for those utilities that

already file that schedule. Similarly, real-time variance information is also already provided during

reporting of final project costs in the Monthly Construction Progress Reports in the Commission’s

report filing portal.


§ 25.192(k) - The PFP includes the requirement for both a non-refundable Interconnection Fee and

Financial Security that points back to those items as defined in § 25.194, which is being devised

in Project No. 58481. In keeping with the AEP Companies’ comments in that project, the AEP

Companies do not support an offset to rate base due to the negative financial implications they

create for utilities. However, as proposed in § 25.192(k), the offset to revenue requirement is a

more palatable approach for utilities. The AEP Companies appreciate the pivot in approach and

believe it better aligns with appropriate funding of future investment while protecting other

customers.

        The AEP Companies have not proposed a revision to the language in this section, but

recommend that the Commission provide clarity that this offset can be implemented as a credit

rider rather than a literal reduction to the TSP’s transmission cost of service rate. The AEP


Project No. 58000                                                             AEP Companies Comments
                                                  11
 Companies believe that a credit rider could be allowed to be adjusted as new non-refundable Large

Load cash security amounts are accrued and could be a mechanism that can terminate directly at

such time that the monies have all been flowed through to rate payers without need for a full rate

case solely for these purposes. It would also be beneficial for these amounts to be amortized over

a period of time, for example ten years, so that existing customers receive those benefits over time

as this transmission investment begins to flow through customer rates, rather than providing very

short-term rate reductions or volatile rates.

         Additionally, if TSPs will be required to pay interest on the payments pursuant to Texas

Utility Code Chapter 183, to protect from a net interest shortfall, the AEP Companies respectfully

ask that the Commission include a mechanism within the proposed credit rider for any net interest

expense incurred by a TSP to be netted out. More precisely, in the event that the interest rates set

by the Commission exceeds the rate at which a TSP is able to earn comparable return on refundable

amounts, the AEP Companies respectfully ask that the Commission allow the portion of interest

expense calculated as the difference between the statutory interest rate and TSPs actual earned rate

be incorporated in the credit rider.8 The rule should neither benefit nor disadvantage the TSP, so

alternatively, if the Commission is opposed to this net interest recommendation, the AEP

Companies respectfully ask that the Commission clarify in this rulemaking that Texas Utility Code

Chapter 183 provisions do not apply to these payments from Large Load customers.

         The AEP Companies recommend that the Commission address this issue and specify that

this mechanism is permissible in the Proposal for Adoption or its preamble.




         8
             Public Utility Commission of Texas, Historical Interest Rates Applicable to Utility Deposits, available at
https://ftp.puc.texas.gov/public/puct-info/industry/electric/reports/HRates/HistRates.pdf, accessed August 10, 2026.

Project No. 58000                                                                         AEP Companies Comments
                                                          12
     B. § 25.193 Distribution Service Provider TCRF

§ 25.193(c) - The last variable in the TCRF table purports to use a “projected billing determinant.”

To date, all billing determinants that go into the formula are based on historical data. The revised

definition of Billing Determinant (BD) in the TCRF formula changes the current billing

determinant definition of kilowatt-hour (kWh) or kilowatt (kW) or kilovolt-ampere (kVa) for all

customer classes to the class, “…BD is each class’s projected billing determinants for the time

period the TCRF is expected to be in place, including each Large Load customer’s minimum

billing demands in lieu of the Large Load customer’s actual 12CP billing demand where that

customer’s 12CP demand is less than that customer’s Large Load minimum billing demand.” AEP

Texas agrees with the change that matches the TCRF class billing determinants to the length of

time the TCRF is expected to be in place either via the semi-annual filings or UTM tracker filing

time frames for TCRF recovery. AEP Texas does have a concern with “projecting” billing

determinants over that same period. Currently, depending on the TCRF rate class, a TCRF billing

determinant of kWh or NCP demand or 4CP (12CP) demand is used for billing TCRF charges to

the Retail Electric Providers. Projecting billing determinants is unnecessary. The Commission is

transitioning to a 12CP load for load ratio share purposes in the ERCOT matrix, the allocation of

transmission service costs through the TCRF, and billing demands for those customers that are

billed under the 4CP (12CP) billing determinant (in addition to the Large Load minimum demands

or 12CP). The historical 12CP billing determinant and the Large Load minimum contract demand

are known quantities.

        Since the historic 12CP will be used for all of the 12CP demand-billed TCRF classes

including the Secondary > 10 kW 12CP, Primary Distribution Line 12CP, Primary Substation

12CP, and the Transmission Voltage class, it would not make sense to project the TCRF billing



Project No. 58000                                                           AEP Companies Comments
                                                13
 determinants of the other classes that use kWh and NCP-based billing demand. Ideally, the 12CP

loads and the Large Load minimum demands as published by ERCOT and approved by the

Commission should be used to adjust the TCRF class allocators and accommodate the class Large

Load billing determinants. Keeping the TCRF allocators and class billing determinants in sync

will isolate the Large Load cost allocation to the class associated with the Large Loads and protect

other customers that share a TCRF class with the Large Loads by neutralizing the TCRF rate for

that class using the minimum billing demands on the allocation side and the billing determinant

side. AEP Texas does not anticipate the need to project TCRF class billing determinants.

        Proposed Redline

          BD is each class’s projected billing determinants for the time period the TCRF is expected
          to be in place, including each large load customer’s minimum billing demands in lieu of
          the large load customer’s actual 12CP billing demand where that customer’s 12CP
          billing demand is less than that customer’s large load minimum billing demand.


    C. § 25.252 Large Load Customer Tariffs

§ 25.252(e) – The AEP Companies are generally supportive of Staff's analysis of separate treatment

for Large Loads and the inclusion of a minimum demand charge recommendation, which has been

adopted and is actively being considered in tariff structures and contracts across other jurisdictions.

In addition to the proposed minimum demand charge and minimum contract term, the AEP

Companies offer that additional provisions including a type of collateral requirement and a defined

notice period imposed to terminate service coupled with an exit fee would help ensure that other

customer classes are not harmed if a Large Load customer does not remain online for the duration

of the proposed 20-year minimum contract term.

        Long-term commitments help ensure that an appropriate proportion of asset investments

undertaken to serve a Large Load customer are borne by that customer, reducing the risk of cost


Project No. 58000                                                             AEP Companies Comments
                                                  14
 shifting. Ramp-up periods provide flexibility during load development while still preserving cost

causation over time. Finally, termination fees and financial assurances protect other customers

from bearing unrecovered costs if a Large Load departs prior to the end of its contracted term.

These types of financial commitments reasonably recognize and align with the financial

commitments that will be required by the utilities to provide these customers with service. Large

Load tariffs in other states that have been designed with these types of additional provisions fairly

balance the interests of new Large Load customers and the utilities with the obligation to construct

facilities to serve them, while also ensuring existing customers are protected.

        Similar to security held during the study and construction periods, collateral requirements

could be implemented to protect against financial risk if a Large Load customer unexpectedly stops

taking service. In states with vertically integrated utilities, the collateral/security required is

typically 24 months of non-fuel revenues. The AEP Companies submit that a period of two to five

years of collateral could be required to ensure these Large Loads continue to cover the investment

required to serve them while providing a period of time for a utility to potentially find another

customer willing to take on the capacity no longer being used by the customer. This construct

supports the policy shift in ERCOT toward the allocation of capacity while also allowing a path

forward for the Large Load customer that is connected and utilizing the grid. If there is not a Large

Load customer able to receive the capacity, the original Large Load customer would remain

responsible until their number of minimum bills is complete and should pay that amount as a

termination or exit fee. The AEP Companies propose new rules §§ 25.252(e)(3) and (e)(4) to

implement this concept.

        Proposed Redline

        (3)     Collateral Required. Upon execution of the interconnection agreement
                contemplated in (c)(3), the large load customer must provide an amount of


Project No. 58000                                                            AEP Companies Comments
                                                 15
                 collateral equal to 24 times the minimum billing demand based bill. The amount of
                collateral to be held will be recomputed annually and updated if the recomputed
                value is 10% greater than the current amount held. Such collateral will be held by
                the DSP.

        (4)     Termination Fee. If large load customer terminates its interconnection agreement
                prior to the end of the Minimum Term or any Renewal Term, whether by declaring
                large load customer’s intent to terminate or by failing to comply with any material
                terms of the interconnection agreement, including, but not limited to, payment of
                the full amount due under the agreement, for a period of three months, then large
                load customer shall owe and pay to interconnecting DSP within 90 days of such
                termination an amount equal to the future minimum payments due under the
                agreement, for the remaining portions of the interconnection agreement.



                                       IV.     CONCLUSION

        The AEP Companies appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the Commission’s

Proposal for Publication in Project No. 58000. The revisions proposed by the AEP Companies are

intended to clarify aspects of the rule, identify areas where alignment or consistency may be

necessary with other rules or rulemakings, and support the objectives of SB 6 and direction from

the Office of the Texas Governor. The AEP Companies look forward to continued participation in

the process.

 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                             §

                        AEP COMPANIES’ EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

       The AEP Companies respectfully submit these comments in response to the Commission’s
Proposal for Publication (PFP) revising16 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) § 25.192 and
25.193, and proposing new 16 TAC § 25.252, in support of the rulemaking but believe certain
provisions of the PFP would benefit from revisions to better specify processes related to Large
Loads and associated cost recovery, and protection of ratepayers in other customer classes. The
AEP Companies recommend the following key revisions such that the Commission:

    •   clarify that the definition of Transmission Interconnection Costs proposed in both § 25.192
        and § 25.252 is intended to capture retail loads equal to or greater than 75MW only, not
        other, smaller retail loads or other non-retail Transmission Service Customers such as
        generators and other utilities;

    •   add a collateral requirement and termination fee to the Large Load Customer Tariff
        proposed in § 25.252 to better protect other customer classes if a Large Load departs prior

                    II.    RESPONSES TO OUESTIONS FOR COMMENT

        The AEP Companies provide responses to the Commission's specific questions included

in the PFP below.

    1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions
       be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
       different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

        No. A minimum demand charge ensures that Large Load customers are responsible for the

transmission investment caused by their demand on the system, rather than only being responsible

for their energy usage. Implementing minimum billing demand provisions is consistent with the

directives in Governor Abbott' s June 10, 2026 letter to the Commission and ERCOT. The AEP


Project No. 58000                                                         AEP Companies Comments
                                                2
 Companies support a minimum billing demand provision that applies to all Large Load customers

in the same manner and is based on each customer's contracted peak demand, not its non-

coincident peak (NCP) demand. This approach will ensure that all Large Load customers are

equally accountable to the capacity that they have reserved and align to the actual driver of costs

because transmission and distribution infrastructure is planned and built to serve the capacity that

a customer reserves. A utility commits capital based on contracted peak demand, not on what the

customer happens to draw in any given interval. Under an NCP scenario, a Large Load could

reserve substantial capacity, causing the serving utility to build significant infrastructure to meet

that maximum load. If a Large Load customer ramps slowly or underutilizes their contracted

demand, that customer could pay far below the cost of the infrastructure dedicated to serving them,

resulting in other classes being allocated those costs. The use of contracted peak demand better

matches the cost to the customer who requested the level of service driving the infrastructure

investment.

    2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
          a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
          b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
          c. extended to a longer time period?

        In Project No. 58484, the AEP Companies provided comments on minimum billing

demand contract terms. As described in those comments, the other AEP affiliates have Large Load

tariffs in place that include fixed contract periods of 12-20 years. The AEP Companies support a

minimum billing demand period that is consistent with cost-causation arguments and the overall

recent policy directives to balance Large Load development and non-Large Load customer

interests. One challenge the AEP Companies have identified with the minimum billing demand

construct currently set forth in the PFP, as compared to its affiliates' tariffs, is that the PFP does

not include some other key provisions of a Large Load tariff such as a collateral requirement and


Project No. 58000                                                            AEP Companies Comments
                                                  3
 defined exit fee with a notice requirement that helps ensure that other ratepayers are held harmless

if a Large Load customer ceases taking service before the minimum billing demand period expires.

The AEP Companies recommend that the Commission consider adding these key provisions to the

rule as discussed further below and in the AEP Companies' comments in Project No. 58484.

    3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
       lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
       load minimum billing demand:
           a. reflect a "ratcheted" demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand
              is some percentage of the customer's contracted peak demand or maximum
              NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline
              in phases over the years, and how?
           b. be based on a "weighted average" minimum billing demand, wherein the large
              load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
              customer's contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
              year and the large load customer's 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
              weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
              over the years, and how?

        As stated in the response to Question 1, the AEP Companies believe the minimum billing

demand should be based on contracted peak demand. It is a floor the customer pays regardless of

actual usage. Transmission and distribution infrastructure is planned and constructed to serve the

capacity reserved by the customer, and contracted peak demand provides the most direct link

between the customer's service request and the investment required to serve that request.

Accordingly, the AEP Companies do not support basing the minimum billing demand on a

measure lower than contracted peak demand.

        Ideally, the minimum billing demand would be based on the contract peak demand until

such time that the Large Load customer' s 12CP demand exceeds the minimum contract demand.

In that instance there is no need for the adoption of an NCP minimum billing demand or ratchet

given that the average prior year 12CP is based on a 100% ratchet. If the Commission were to

adopt an NCP-based approach, the AEP Companies believe a ratchet mechanism would be

preferable to relying solely on actual usage because it would establish a billing floor that Large

Project No. 58000                                                           AEP Companies Comments
                                                 4
 Loads must pay regardless of usage and reduce the potential for a customer to lower its obligation

through temporary curtailment after establishing peak demand level.

        The AEP Companies do not recommend a weighted average minimum billing demand.

Such an approach would add complexity without providing meaningful improvement in cost

causation or cost recovery as compared to either a contracted peak demand framework or an

NCP-based framework.

    4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as
        an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
        Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
        electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
        cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include
        applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large
        computational loads.

        Separate rate treatment for large computational load should take into account applicable

Texas statutes and Commission rules that govern rates, rate classes, and tariffs. Under PURA §

36.003(b), a rate may not be unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory but must be

sufficient, equitable, and consistent in application to each class of consumer. In addition, PURA §

36.003(c) prohibits an electric utility from (1) granting an unreasonable preference or advantage

concerning rates to a person in a classification; (2) subjecting a person in a classification to an

unreasonable prejudice or disadvantage concerning rates; or (3) establishing or maintaining an

unreasonable difference concerning rates between localities or between classes of service.

Separate rate treatment for computational loads, such as data centers, would create a new

classification of a consumer and rates charged to that new classification would need to be evaluated

under PURA § 36.003. If separate rate treatment for computational loads was implemented, large

load requirements may not be consistently applied to all customers meeting the applicable

threshold unless the Commission determines there is a reasonable basis for treating computational

loads differently than other Large Loads. Section 32.101 of PURA requires electric utilities to file

Project No. 58000                                                           AEP Companies Comments
                                                 5
 official tariffs showing all rates, rules, and classifications with each regulatory authority. An

electric utility may not directly or indirectly charge, demand, or receive from a person a greater or

lesser compensation for a service provided or to be provided by the utility than the compensation

prescribed by the applicable tariff filed under Section 32.101.4 The statutory definition of "rate"

encompasses a tariff while Commission rules more specifically address a tariff as a utility' s

schedule containing all rates and charges stated separately by type of service.6 Commission rules

also define rate class as a group of customers taking electric service under the same rate schedule.7

The AEP Companies also note that SB 6 does not require separate rate treatment for a specific

subset ofLarge Load customers, rather it addresses all loads of 75 MW or greater. The Commission

could incorporate any rate-related specifics of large computational loads into an existing rate

schedule with additional distinct terms and conditions that applied to these loads.

    5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
       transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to

        No, the definition of Transmission Interconnection Costs should not be broadened to

include transmission projects identified through the batch study process. As discussed further

below, the AEP Companies believe the definition should be limited to customer-specific

interconnection facilities and should be clarified to apply to facilities constructed solely to

interconnect a Large Load customer to the transmission system. Broader transmission network

upgrades identified through transmission planning processes provide system-wide benefits and

serve multiple current or future customers over time. Expanding the definition to include such

facilities would make it very challenging for transmission providers to assign network upgrades to

           If Large Loads are able to receive a capacity allocation, as contemplated in the Batch

                        AEP COMPANIES' EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

        The AEP Companies respectfully submit these comments in response to the Commission' s
Proposal for Publication (PFP) revisingl6 Texas Administrative Code ("TAC") § 25.192 and
25.193, and proposing new 16 TAC § 25.252, in support of the rulemaking but believe certain
provisions of the PFP would benefit from revisions to better specify processes related to Large
Loads and associated cost recovery, and protection of ratepayers in other customer classes. The
AEP Companies recommend the following key revisions such that the Commission:

    •   clarify that the definition of Transmission Interconnection Costs proposed in both § 25.192
        and § 25.252 is intended to capture retail loads equal to or greater than 75MW only, not
        other, smaller retail loads or other non-retail Transmission Service Customers such as
        generators and other utilities;

    •   add a collateral requirement and termination fee to the Large Load Customer Tariff
        proposed in § 25.252 to better protect other customer classes if a Large Load departs prior
        to the end of its contracted term;

    •   revert the proposed change to "projected" billing determinant in § 25.193 for the revised
        definition of Billing Determinant (BD) in the TCRF formula, as it is unnecessary over time;

    •   clarify the definition of 12CP Intervals to allow for aggregation of data currently polled at
        15-minute intervals into 30-minute intervals, and that reprogramming or in-person updates
        of 15-minute meters is not contemplated;

    •   revise the definition ERCOT 12CP proposed in § 25.192 to include behind-the-meter loads;

    •   allow the offset to revenue requirement contemplated in § 25.192 from non-refundable
        Interconnection Fees or Financial Security to be implemented as a credit rider rather than
        a literal reduction to the TSP's TCOS rate, and that this credit rider include net interest
        expense, and be adjusted as these monies accrue, outside of a full base rate case.
